newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FOCUS-Bank of Israel holds key rate, watches CPI.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bank of Israel holds key rate, watches CPI.

text.p: The Bank of Israel on Monday said it would leave its key lending rate for August unchanged at an annual 12.7 percent to get a better idea of how inflation is moving.
The decision followed last month's sharp reduction of 1.2 percentage points in the rate, which is charged to commercial banks at daily and weekly tenders.

"We decided to keep rates unchanged this month in a desire to see greater clarity of the picture, especially in view of the fact that recently additional policy measures have been annnounced," Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel told Reuters.

"We will need to see how the markets continue to absorb them and, especially in this context, we will need to examine the implication of these measures on inflation forecasts," Frenkel said in an interview.
He referred to last month's changes to the exchange rate regime, which led to a depreciation of about four percent in the shekel, and to an easing of foreign currency controls.
The government also agreed recently to cut the 1997 budget by 800 million shekels ($226 million).
June's consumer price index rose by a surprisingly steep 1.1 percent, bringing inflation in the past 12 months to 8.4 percent. The government's 1997 inflation target is 7-10 percent.
"Our approach in setting interest rates is cast in a medium term perspective rather than influenced by a single monthly index," Frenkel said.

"It is obvious we will need to continue monitoring developments on the inflation front and make assessments on the likelihood that the inflation target set by the govenrment is being met," Frenkel said.
He noted that capital markets' inflationary expectations, which the central bank monitors closely, had risen recently. They now stand at 9.7 percent for the coming 12 months.

"We will need to verify if this indicates a new trend which will need to be countered...or whether it represents a temporary reaction to the last monthly price index which was higher than initially expected. Much of this dust should settle within the next month," Frenkel said.
Financial markets had anticipated Monday's decision.
"The market did not expect a change in rates and the decision will not affect trading on Tuesday," said Julien Assous of Sahar Securities.
Ilan Shabat, an investment adviser at Israel Discount Bank, called the decision "a wise one" and said the market could use this as an excuse to continue its rise, at least for now.
But he warned that the effect of the Israeli currency's depreciation on inflation was uncertain. "If the dollar continues to rise we may have an interest rate hike in the future," Shabat said.
